subtopic_detail: A toddler refusing to use an arm after being swung by the hands, but with elbow swelling and bony point tenderness
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a two year old girl brought in an hour after an afternoon at the park. Her grandmother says she was swung between two adults by her hands and afterwards would not use her left arm.

She holds the arm at her side, slightly bent with the palm turned down, and cries when anyone tries to move it. When you ask the grandmother to walk you through the afternoon she adds that the child had also come off the bottom of the slide onto the grass at some point but seemed fine at the time. On examination there is visible swelling over the outer side of the left elbow and she screams and pulls away when you press over the bony prominence there. The forearm and wrist are not swollen or tender and the skin is intact. Her radial pulse is present and her fingers are warm with normal capillary refill and normal movement.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held adducted, elbow slightly flexed and forearm pronated, swelling over the lateral elbow with marked point tenderness over the lateral bony prominence, no forearm or wrist tenderness, intact skin, radial pulse present with normal capillary refill and finger movement
data_table.Growth: Weight and height on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Perform a hyperpronation manoeuvre and reassess her arm after fifteen minutes
options.rationale: Reduction is appropriate for the classic presentation, which has a clear axial traction mechanism with no swelling and no bony tenderness, and manipulating an undiagnosed fracture risks displacing it. Swelling and focal tenderness over the lateral condyle are precisely the findings that remove this option (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow).

options.text: Arrange elbow radiographs before attempting any reduction manoeuvre
options.rationale: Radial head subluxation produces no swelling and no bony point tenderness, so their presence together with an added fall from a slide means a lateral condylar or supracondylar fracture must be excluded before any manipulation. Lateral condylar fractures are intra articular, are easily missed on a single view and displace if managed as a pulled elbow (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow).

options.text: Apply a broad arm sling and review her in the fracture clinic next week
options.rationale: Deferring assessment for a week risks displacement of an undiagnosed intra articular fracture, which converts a cast into an operation. Immobilisation without imaging also leaves both the diagnosis and the neurovascular monitoring plan undefined (Source: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region

options.text: Perform a supination and flexion manoeuvre and then apply a collar and cuff
options.rationale: This is the alternative reduction technique, differing from hyperpronation only in success rate and comfort, and it carries the same objection here because the examination does not fit radial head subluxation. Splinting afterwards would also mask the failure of a manoeuvre that should not have been attempted (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow).

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound of the elbow to look for a joint effusion first
options.rationale: Ultrasound can demonstrate an effusion but does not characterise the fracture line, its displacement or the involvement of the articular surface, all of which determine management. Plain films answer the question that has been raised (Source: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation is the commonest elbow injury in children under five and follows sudden axial traction on a pronated forearm, classically when a child is lifted or swung by the hand. The diagnosis rests on a typical mechanism with a completely normal examination apart from refusal to use the arm, and radiographs are unnecessary when that pattern is clear because reduction is both diagnostic and therapeutic. What makes the diagnosis unsafe is any swelling, bruising, deformity or bony point tenderness, or a mechanism involving a fall, since lateral condylar and supracondylar fractures present in the same age group with a similarly held arm. Lateral condylar fractures are Salter Harris type IV injuries that cross the articular surface, are frequently subtle on the anteroposterior view and progress to non union and cubitus valgus if missed. Documented neurovascular status before and after any manipulation is part of the record in every case.
key_points: Radial head subluxation shows no swelling, bruising or bony tenderness
Any swelling or point tenderness mandates radiographs before manipulation
A fall as part of the mechanism removes the classic history
Lateral condylar fractures are intra articular and are easily missed on one view
Reduction is diagnostic and therapeutic only when the presentation is typical
explanation.pearls: After a successful reduction a child with radial head subluxation usually begins using the arm again within five to ten minutes, and continued refusal to use the arm at thirty minutes should prompt radiographs rather than a repeat manoeuvre.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region

subtopic_detail: Dark urine and severe thigh pain three days after a first high intensity gym session with a dipstick positive for blood and no red cells
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 21 year old man with three days of severe pain and swelling in both thighs. He attended his first high intensity gym class four days ago and did several hundred repeated squats, and he could barely walk the next morning.

He tells you his wee has gone the colour of dark tea for the past two days and that he has passed less of it than usual. He takes no regular medication, uses no supplements or recreational drugs, and has never had anything like this before. On examination both thighs are diffusely swollen and tender to palpation, but the compartments are soft, passive knee extension does not produce disproportionate pain and his distal pulses and sensation are normal. His urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, and microscopy of the same sample shows no red cells. His creatine kinase is 48200 U/L and his creatinine is 138 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 102 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 48200 U/L (30-200), creatinine 138 micromol/L (60-110), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), corrected calcium 1.98 mmol/L (2.20-2.65), phosphate 1.7 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-32), urine dipstick strongly positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy
data_table.Examination: Both thighs diffusely swollen and tender with soft compartments, no disproportionate pain on passive knee extension, normal distal pulses, sensation and capillary refill

lead_in: What is the most important initial treatment?

options.text: Start intravenous frusemide to establish and maintain a good urine output
options.rationale: A loop diuretic produces urine at the expense of intravascular volume, worsening the renal hypoperfusion that is driving the injury, and it acidifies the urine which favours cast formation. Urine output here is restored by filling the patient rather than by driving the kidney (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Start an intravenous sodium bicarbonate infusion to alkalinise the urine
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation is theoretically attractive because myoglobin casts form more readily in acid urine, but no trial has shown benefit over sodium chloride alone and it aggravates the hypocalcaemia already present. It is a considered adjunct rather than the initial treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate to correct his low serum calcium level
options.rationale: Calcium is sequestered in injured muscle during the acute phase and is released back into the circulation during recovery, so replacing it in an asymptomatic patient predisposes to rebound hypercalcaemia and metastatic calcification. Calcium is given only for symptomatic hypocalcaemia or for cardiac membrane stabilisation in severe hyperkalaemia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Refer him for urgent haemodialysis to clear the circulating myoglobin load
options.rationale: Myoglobin is poorly cleared by conventional dialysis and its removal is not the reason dialysis is used in this condition, which is refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemia. None of those thresholds is met with a potassium of 5.4 mmol/L and a bicarbonate of 19 mmol/L (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Acute kidney injury).
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Acute kidney injury

options.text: Start high volume intravenous sodium chloride titrated to urine output
options.rationale: A dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy identifies myoglobin, and early aggressive isotonic crystalloid is the only intervention shown to reduce the incidence of acute kidney injury by maintaining renal perfusion and flushing pigment casts from the tubules. Rates of 1 to 2 litres per hour initially, targeting a urine output of about 200 to 300 mL per hour, are typical until the creatine kinase falls (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Acute kidney injury).
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Acute kidney injury

explanation.summary: Rhabdomyolysis is defined biochemically rather than clinically, with a creatine kinase above about five times the upper limit of normal and typically above 5000 U/L in cases at risk of renal injury. The classic triad of muscle pain, weakness and dark urine is present in fewer than half of cases, and the dipstick discrepancy of blood positive with no red cells on microscopy is the finding that makes the diagnosis at the bedside. Common Australian causes are unaccustomed exertion, prolonged immobility after a fall or overdose, seizures, statins interacting with other drugs, sympathomimetic drugs and hyperthermia. The electrolyte pattern is hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia and early hypocalcaemia from calcium entering damaged muscle, with late rebound hypercalcaemia during recovery. Volume replacement started early is the treatment that matters, and compartment syndrome must be excluded in any swollen limb because it both causes and complicates the condition.
key_points: A dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy indicates myoglobin
Early high volume isotonic crystalloid is the only intervention proven to protect the kidney
Loop diuretics worsen renal hypoperfusion and are avoided
Hypocalcaemia is not corrected unless symptomatic because of rebound during recovery
Dialysis is used for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis or overload, not to clear myoglobin
explanation.pearls: Target a urine output of about 200 to 300 mL per hour and continue fluids until the creatine kinase falls below roughly 5000 U/L, checking the level at least daily, because the peak often occurs one to three days after the muscle injury rather than at presentation.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia: Acute kidney injury

subtopic_detail: An intensely itchy blistering eruption beginning around the umbilicus at 32 weeks with normal liver biochemistry
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 31 year old woman at 32 weeks in her second pregnancy with a two week history of an intensely itchy rash. It started as raised red patches immediately around her navel and has spread outward across her abdomen and onto both thighs.

Over the past four days the patches have developed tense fluid filled blisters up to a centimetre across, several of which have burst and crusted. Her first pregnancy four years ago was uncomplicated with no skin problems. On examination there are urticarial plaques with tense bullae distributed over the periumbilical skin, flanks and proximal thighs, with the umbilicus itself clearly involved, and her abdominal striae are spared. Her palms, soles, face and mucous membranes are clear. Her serum bile acids, transaminases and full blood count are all within normal limits, and foetal growth and the cardiotocograph are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 86 per minute, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent, temperature 36.8 degrees C, foetal heart rate 148 per minute
data_table.Examination: Urticarial plaques with tense bullae over the periumbilical skin, flanks and proximal thighs, umbilicus involved, striae spared, palms soles face and mucosae clear, extensive excoriation
data_table.Investigations: Serum bile acids and transaminases within normal limits, full blood count with eosinophils 0.7 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), urine dipstick negative for protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure her this is a benign pregnancy rash and prescribe a topical steroid
options.rationale: The common benign eruption of pregnancy begins in the abdominal striae and characteristically spares a rim of skin around the umbilicus, which is the reverse of the distribution here, and it does not produce tense bullae. Treating without a diagnosis also misses the neonatal and maternal implications that follow from the alternative (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy).

options.text: Measure serum bile acids and plan birth at 37 weeks for her symptoms
options.rationale: Cholestasis of pregnancy causes itch without any primary rash and her bile acids and transaminases are already normal, so repeating them adds nothing. A visible blistering eruption directs the workup to the skin rather than the liver (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy).

options.text: Prescribe an oral antihistamine with emollients and review her in two weeks
options.rationale: Antihistamines and emollients provide only partial symptom relief in a blistering autoimmune eruption, which usually requires systemic corticosteroid, and a two week delay allows further blistering and excoriation. Symptomatic treatment without histology also leaves the foetal surveillance plan unmade (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy).

options.text: Arrange a skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin
options.rationale: Tense bullae arising from urticarial plaques centred on the umbilicus with sparing of the striae is the pattern of an autoimmune blistering disease of pregnancy, and linear complement C3 deposition along the basement membrane on direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin is the diagnostic finding. Confirming it matters because the condition is associated with foetal growth restriction and preterm birth, needs systemic corticosteroid, and produces a transient blistering rash in around 10 per cent of newborns (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy).

options.text: Arrange induction of labour this week to bring the rash to an end
options.rationale: Birth at 32 weeks for a maternal skin condition trades established prematurity against a rash that is treatable with corticosteroid, and the eruption commonly flares at delivery in any case rather than resolving immediately. Serial growth surveillance with treatment is the appropriate response (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Dermatoses of pregnancy).
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Dermatoses of pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pemphigoid gestationis is a rare autoimmune blistering disease driven by antibodies against collagen XVII in the hemidesmosome, usually presenting in the second or third trimester with intense itch and urticarial plaques that begin at the umbilicus and evolve into tense bullae. Its principal differential is polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, which begins in abdominal striae, spares the umbilicus, occurs typically in a first pregnancy or a multiple pregnancy, and does not blister. Diagnosis is by direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin showing linear C3 along the basement membrane zone, with circulating antibodies detectable on indirect testing. Treatment is potent topical corticosteroid for mild disease and systemic prednisolone for extensive or blistering disease, and pregnancies are monitored for growth restriction and preterm birth. The condition characteristically flares at the time of birth, recurs in subsequent pregnancies often earlier and more severely, and can flare with the combined oral contraceptive pill or menstruation.
key_points: Umbilical involvement with tense bullae distinguishes it from polymorphic eruption of pregnancy
Polymorphic eruption begins in the striae and spares the umbilicus without blistering
Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows linear C3 at the basement membrane
Associated with foetal growth restriction and preterm birth, so growth surveillance is needed
About one in ten neonates develop a transient blistering rash that resolves spontaneously
explanation.pearls: Warn the woman that the eruption typically flares in the days around birth rather than settling, and that it can recur with menstruation or the combined oral contraceptive pill, so a progestogen only or non hormonal method is preferred afterwards.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Dermatoses of pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Repeated admissions for events witnessed only by one parent across three hospitals, with every investigation normal
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked by the paediatric team to review the family of a four year old boy admitted for the fifth time this year with reported episodes in which he stops breathing and shakes.

The paediatric team has established that he has had eleven admissions across three hospitals in two states, and that a gastrostomy was inserted at another hospital eighteen months ago for reported feeding difficulty. His growth is on the 50th centile and he eats enthusiastically on the ward. Five days of video electroencephalogram monitoring has captured no abnormal electrical activity and no clinical event, and his metabolic screen, echocardiogram and sleep study are all normal. Nursing notes record that every reported episode over the admission has occurred while his mother was alone with him and none has been witnessed by staff. His mother, who worked for several years as an enrolled nurse, is present continuously, is attentive and well liked, and is asking for a referral to a fourth neurologist interstate.

data_table.Examination: Well grown and developmentally appropriate four year old, eating normally on the ward, gastrostomy in situ with no local complication, normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: Five day video electroencephalogram with no abnormal activity and no captured event, metabolic screen, echocardiogram and polysomnography all within normal limits
data_table.Collateral: Eleven admissions across three hospitals in two states, all reported episodes unwitnessed by staff and occurring when one carer was alone with the child

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discuss your concerns directly with the mother and seek her explanation today
options.rationale: Early confrontation before a coordinated plan is in place commonly precipitates removal of the child from hospital, transfer to another health service and escalation of the reported symptoms, all of which increase risk. Any conversation with the family happens after the statutory notification and within an agreed multidisciplinary plan (Source: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child).
source_refs: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child

options.text: Arrange covert video surveillance of the cubicle to document what happens
options.rationale: Covert surveillance raises significant legal and ethical problems, requires police and executive authorisation where it is used at all, and is never the initial step taken by a treating team. The threshold for notification is reasonable suspicion of harm, which has already been reached without it (Source: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child).
source_refs: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child

options.text: Notify the state child protection service and convene a multidisciplinary meeting
options.rationale: Doctors are mandatory reporters in every Australian state and territory and the threshold is a reasonable belief of significant harm, which is met by invasive procedures and repeated admissions for events that only ever occur in one person's presence with uniformly normal investigations. Convening the treating teams, the general practitioner and child protection assembles the chronology from all services, which is the single most important diagnostic step in these cases (Source: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child).
source_refs: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child

options.text: Refer the mother for psychiatric assessment before taking any other action
options.rationale: There is no consistent psychiatric profile in these cases and a normal assessment of the carer does not lower the risk to the child, so making the referral the gateway step delays protection. Assessment of the carer has a place later, within the child protection plan rather than ahead of it (Source: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child).
source_refs: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child

options.text: Arrange a further prolonged video electroencephalogram before deciding
options.rationale: Ordering more of an investigation that has already been comprehensively normal continues the pattern of escalating intervention that is itself the harm, and each admission carries its own risks. Further testing is warranted only if a new clinical finding emerges (Source: Royal Children's Hospital: Child abuse and neglect).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital: Child abuse and neglect

explanation.summary: Fabricated or induced illness is a form of child abuse in which a carer exaggerates, fabricates or produces symptoms and signs, leading to unnecessary and often invasive medical intervention. The signature features are a history that only one person can corroborate, symptoms that resolve when the carer is absent, investigations that are persistently normal, multiple hospitals and specialists involved, and a carer who is unusually comfortable in the medical environment and who pushes for further procedures. It is a diagnosis about the child's care rather than about the carer's psychopathology, so the assessment focuses on assembling a chronology of all health contacts across services rather than on interviewing the carer. Australian doctors are mandatory reporters and the threshold for notification is a reasonable belief of significant harm, not proof. Mortality is estimated at around 6 to 10 per cent and siblings are at risk, so any notification asks about them as well.
key_points: Events witnessed by only one carer with consistently normal investigations is the core pattern
The chronology assembled across all health services is the key diagnostic instrument
Notification requires reasonable belief of harm, not proof, and doctors are mandatory reporters
Confrontation before a coordinated plan increases risk to the child
Siblings should be considered in any notification
explanation.pearls: Request the records from every hospital and general practice involved before speaking with the family, because the diagnosis is usually made by seeing eleven admissions in one place rather than by any single clinical finding, and each service typically knows about only its own two or three.

sources.label: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child
Royal Children's Hospital: Child abuse and neglect

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of nappy area rash unresponsive to barrier cream that now involves the skin creases with satellite lesions
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a nine month old boy whose mother has brought him with a nappy rash that has been present for three weeks. She has been using a thick zinc barrier cream at every change and changing him promptly, and it looked better for a few days but has since spread.

The rash is now bright red and shiny, and she says he cries when she wipes him. On examination the erythema is confluent across the buttocks and perineum and extends deep into the inguinal and gluteal creases, and there are small separate red papules and a few pustules on the lower abdomen and inner thighs beyond the main area of redness. The skin is not eroded or ulcerated and there is no surrounding cellulitis or fluctuance. Looking in his mouth there are white plaques on his tongue and inner cheeks that do not wipe away easily. He is afebrile, feeding normally and growing along the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: Confluent bright erythema across the buttocks and perineum extending into the inguinal and gluteal creases, satellite papules and pustules on the lower abdomen and inner thighs, no erosion or ulceration, no cellulitis, adherent white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa
data_table.Growth: Weight and length on the 50th centile with no change over three months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Apply a topical imidazole antifungal cream at every nappy change
options.rationale: Involvement of the skin creases with satellite papules and pustules beyond the main rash, together with adherent oral plaques, indicates candidal infection rather than the irritant dermatitis that barrier cream treats. A topical imidazole applied at each change under the barrier cream is first line, with oral treatment added for the mouth (Source: RCH CPG: Nappy rash).

options.text: Apply a potent topical corticosteroid ointment twice daily for one week
options.rationale: Potent corticosteroids are avoided in the nappy area because occlusion under a nappy greatly increases absorption, risking skin atrophy and adrenal suppression, and they worsen an untreated fungal infection. A short course of hydrocortisone 1 per cent is the only steroid used here, and only for stubborn inflammation alongside antifungal treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Nappy rash).

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for five days and continue the barrier cream
options.rationale: Bacterial infection of the nappy area presents with pustules, honey coloured crusting, erosions or surrounding cellulitis, none of which is present, and satellite lesions with crease involvement point elsewhere. Oral antibiotics would also further disturb the flora that allows overgrowth (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Continue the barrier cream at every change and review him in two weeks
options.rationale: Barrier preparations treat irritant dermatitis, which characteristically spares the creases because urine and faeces do not reach them, and three weeks of adequate use has already failed. Persisting adds another fortnight of discomfort without addressing the organism (Source: RCH CPG: Nappy rash).

options.text: Prescribe oral fluconazole as a single dose and continue the barrier cream
options.rationale: Systemic antifungal treatment is reserved for extensive, recurrent or immunocompromised disease because topical treatment clears uncomplicated candidal nappy dermatitis, and a single dose would in any case not cover the treatment period needed. It differs from the preferred option mainly in exposing him to systemic drug effects for no added benefit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

explanation.summary: Nappy rash is most often an irritant contact dermatitis from prolonged contact with urine and faeces, and it characteristically affects the convex surfaces of the buttocks, thighs and pubic area while sparing the depths of the skin creases. Secondary candidal infection is common after about three days of any nappy rash and is recognised by bright confluent erythema that fills the creases, satellite papules and pustules outside the main area, and often coexisting oral plaques. Bacterial infection, seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis, scabies and, rarely, zinc deficiency or Langerhans cell histiocytosis are the other diagnoses to hold in mind, and a rash that is eroded, ulcerated or fails to respond to appropriate treatment should prompt reconsideration. Management always includes frequent nappy changes, nappy free time, gentle cleansing without soap and a barrier preparation, with a topical imidazole added when candidal features are present. Potent corticosteroids are avoided because the nappy acts as an occlusive dressing.
key_points: Irritant dermatitis spares the skin creases while candidal infection fills them
Satellite papules and pustules beyond the main rash indicate candida
Topical imidazole under a barrier preparation is first line treatment
Potent topical steroids are avoided because the nappy occludes and enhances absorption
Oral plaques point to a coexisting oral infection needing separate treatment
explanation.pearls: Treat the mouth at the same time as the nappy area with oral miconazole gel or nystatin, because an untreated oral reservoir passes through the gut and reinfects the nappy area within days of stopping the topical cream.
